newsitem.title: USA: US Senate panel delays nuclear waste bill vote.
newsitem.headline: US Senate panel delays nuclear waste bill vote.

text.p: The U.S. Senate Energy Committee Wednesday put off a vote on a bill to build a temporary nuclear waste dump in Nevada after Democrats raised objections on a procedural rule.

Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, said the objection forced him to cut off the meeting, but said he intended for the committee to vote on the bill tomorrow, after 30 minutes of discussion on amendments.

But Senator Jeff Bingaman, a New Mexico Democrat, said he wanted adequate time to discuss his amendments that would put off building the temporary waste storage facility until after the administration has firmly decided to build a permanent dump in Nevada's Yucca Mountain.
The committee cut off discussion on the bill after an objection was raised that continuing the meeting beyond two hours violated a Senate rule intended to limit morning business.
Murkowski is pushing the bill the Senate passed 63-37 last year to put a temporary nuclear waste dump in Nevada, but which died in the face of President Clinton's threatened veto.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, a few minutes later on the Senate floor, called the objection "at the very least unfortunate" and said it was "not a good sign" for bipartisan cooperation.
Murkowski had hoped to get the bill to the Senate floor next week.
Nevada's two Democratic senators strongly oppose Murkowski's bill, saying it would designate their state as the nation's nuclear dump without fully studying the issue.

But Murkowski and a number of other Republicans say the administration must move quickly to have some place to put the waste from commercial nuclear reactors that the government becomes legally responsible for next year.
Murkowski's bill would have a temporary facility in Nevada start accepting waste in late 1999, a timeframe that Bingaman said was unrealistly tight.
Bingaman's amendment would allow construction of interim storage to start in 2002 if the administration finally decides to build a permanent storage dump at Nevada's Yucca Mountain.
He also called for more environmental review and tighter radiation exposure standards.
